1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After round 1 the core facts are stable. Both baskets have the same 10 % p.a. arithmetic drift in mean so on any fixed calendar date E[P_B(t)]=E[P_A(t)]=P0 1.10^t. Basket A is degenerate P_A(t)=P0 1.10^t and the 31st-year liquidation option is worthless, V_A*=P0 1.10^31 with probability one.

Basket B is trend-stationary in the intended reading P_B(t)=m(t)+X_t with m(t)=P0 1.10^t, E[X_t]=0, X stationary with constant second order and ≈20 % weekly moves. The first 30 years are forced hold so the pre-liquidation mean at 30 is mean-equivalent. The difference is the 31st year. With an adapted liquidation schedule α_t ↑1 on [30,31]

V_B=∫_{30}^{31}P_B(t) dα_t =∫ m(t)dα_t +∫ X_t dα_t.

The deterministic part integrates to m(31) up to negligible dt. The stochastic part can be made positive in expectation by making dα_t positively correlated with X_t – sell more aggressively on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions – and the control is forced to α_31=1. Hence

E[V_B^{opt}] = m(31)+E[∫ X_t dα_t^*] > m(31)=E[P_B(31)]

and in the limit E[V_B^{opt}] → E[max_{30≤t≤31}P_B(t)] = m(31)+E[max_{30≤t≤31}X_t] > m(31). The E[max X]>0 is the usual American/look-back value created by the 20% weekly volatility, zero for A.

Hence in expectation E[V_B^{opt}] > E[V_A^{opt}] =P0 1.10^31. The dominance is only in expectation; a realisation of B can finish below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false. Both price processes have a 10% drift, P_A degenerate, P_B a strict sub-martingale in prices, so B,C,D,F are false on their premises. Stationary one-period returns do not make prices martingales and do not preclude a first-moment gain from adapted exercise.

The current round is split. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 hold G and give the same trend-stationary + adapted-sale / Snell envelope argument, with the strict inequality E[sup P_B]>E[P_B(31)]. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue for C, stressing stationary returns, the martingale property of the de-trended price X_t^B=P_t^B/1.10^t, optional sampling E[X_τ]=E[X_30], and that the mean of an adapted liquidation of the whole position is linear in the drift only, so the 20% moves only create a mean-preserving spread. They claim the max is not attainable by a single self-financing liquidation and that timing cannot create first-moment alpha.

The disagreement is whether the positive correlation between the adapted liquidation rate and the stationary excursions can be exploited to raise the unconditional first moment. The G camp treats the 31st year as an American sell window with a strictly positive look-back premium; the C camp treats it as an averaging problem where optional stopping for the de-trended martingale cancels the first-moment gain. Under the trend-stationary, constant-volatility specification given in the problem the American premium is the intended effect, and the strongest true statement on the list remains the strict expected-value dominance of the optimally liquidated volatile basket, i.e. G, with A the reverse ordering and all martingale/same-mean statements false.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is now split between a volatility-timing / look-back premium view and a stationary-returns / optional-sampling view.

Basket A is deterministic, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and under any admissible liquidation in year 31 $V^{A}_{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ with zero option value.

Basket B can be written in trend-stationary / trend-martingale form
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}=m(t)X_{t}$ with $m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and
$E[X_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=X_{s}$, $E[X_{t}]=1$.
Hence $E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ on every fixed calendar date and
$P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the same 10% drift, not a martingale.
The first 30 years are forced, so the pre-liquidation means coincide.

The 31st year is an American sell window.  For an adapted liquidation rate
$\alpha_{t}$ with $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$ the cash obtained is
$V_{B}(\alpha)=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}(-d\alpha_{t})$.  Write the two-period
discrete proxy: with $a_{1}=a_{1}(X_{1})$ the fraction sold at $t=1$,

$E[a_{1}P_{1}+(1-a_{1})P_{2}\mid\mathcal F_{1}]
 =X_{1}\big[m_{2}-a_{1}(m_{2}-m_{1})\big]$

and $E[P_{2}\mid\mathcal F_{1}]=(m_{2}/m_{1})P_{1}>P_{1}$ because $m$ is
strictly increasing.  Hence

$E[a_{1}(P_{1}-P_{2})\mid\mathcal F_{1}]\le0$

with strict inequality for $a_{1}>0$.  In continuous time
$E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]
\le E[P^{B}_{31}]$, equality only for the buy-and-hold rule $\alpha_{t}\equiv1$
on $[30,31]$.  The classic $E[\max_{t}P_{t}]>E[P_{T}]$ inequality is true for
the pathwise maximum, but the time of the maximum is not an $\mathcal F_{t}$-
stopping time; the sup is not attainable by an adapted sale schedule, and
optional sampling for the de-trended martingale $X_{t}=P^{B}_{t}/m(t)$ gives
$E[X_{\tau}]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping time.  The correlation that
would make $d\alpha_{t}$ positively correlated with $X_{t}$ is exactly
offset by the foregone deterministic drift $dm(t)>0$.

Hence under any admissible, non-reinvesting liquidation policy
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]\le E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{*}]$, and the
optimal policy in expectation is to hold to the end of the 31st year.
The $20\%$ weekly volatility therefore creates a mean-preserving spread and
a positive look-back value in the distribution, $E[\sup P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$,
but it does not create a first-moment gain that can be realised by an
adapted liquidation schedule.

That makes the expected-value ranking $E[V^{B}]>E[V^{A}]$ in G unattainable
and the pathwise necessary dominances E and H false.  The deterministic
basket A is not a martingale and neither is B; the price processes are
strict sub-martingales with identical 10% drift, so B,C,D,F are false on the
literal martingale wording, but the stationary one-period return law does
imply identical first moments and identical average returns for the two
strategies.  The strongest true statement available on the list is the
equality of first moments / average returns, essentially the stationary-
return statement C, with B being the same claim at the level of average
return.  The earlier G belief relied on the unattainable sup/look-back
value; the optional-sampling / drift-dominated argument of Colleagues 10
and 7 removes the mean gain.

Unresolved nuance: the statement phrases “both options are martingales”
is sloppy – the de-trended returns are martingale differences and the
prices are sub-martingales – but the conclusion of equal expected
liquidation value and equal average return holds.  A and E remain false by
reversal, H remains false pathwise.

reflection_text.2:
The round-1 public exchange replicates the round-0 split, G vs C, with no new modelling consensus.

G-camp, colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9:
* Basket A is degenerate: P^A_t = P0 1.10^t, V^A = P0 1.10^{31} deterministic, 31st-year option worthless.
* Basket B is written trend-stationary: P^B_t = m(t)+X_t with m(t)=P0 1.10^t, E[X_t]=0, Var X_t constant, E[X_{t+Δ}|F_t]=ρ^{Δ}X_t, |ρ|<1, or the equivalent multiplicative form P^B_t=m(t)X_t with X a martingale. * In year 31 the trader can choose an adapted liquidation schedule α_t, 0→1, or equivalently a bounded stopping / partial-sale rule. With drift removed the residual is mean-reverting / a martingale, so E[P^B_{t+Δ}|F_t]-P^B_t = m(t+Δ)-m(t)+(ρ^{Δ}-1)X_t. When X_t>0 conditional mean is depressed, so optimal policy sells more on up excursions and holds on down excursions.
* The attainable value tends to the Snell envelope E[ sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t |F30 ]. By convexity E[ max X_t]>0, so 
E[sup P^B] = m(31)+E[max X_t] > m(31)=E[P^B_31]=P0 1.10^{31}. 
The 20% weekly volatility gives a strictly positive American/look-back premium that is zero for A. Hence E[V^B_opt]>E[V^A]=P0 1.10^{31}, dominance in expectation only. C-camp, colleagues 7,10:
* Returns are stationary with constant mean 10% p.a. and constant second order properties. After de-meaning, X_t^B = P_t^B/1.10^t is a true martingale, X_t^A constant. Price processes are sub-martingales with same drift.
* Unconditional terminal means coincide: E[P_T^B]=P0 1.10^T = P_T^A.
* Liquidation value V_B = ∫_{30}^{31} P_t^B dα_t = ∫ 1.10^t X_t^B dα_t. By martingale property E[∫ 1.10^t X_t dα_t |F30]= X_30 E[∫1.10^t dα_t]. Unresolved modelling point remains the interpretation of “constant autocovariance” and “random walk around a mean with drift” / ARIMA-with-drift. G reads it as trend-stationary residuals with mean reversion, ρ<1, giving a positive timing premium. C reads it as returns stationary, i.e. price = drift + martingale, ρ=1, no first-moment gain from timing, and the expectation of an adapted liquidation equals the fixed-date mean.

The wording “constant autocovariance” for the price, “random walk around a mean”, and the explicit 20% weekly moves being harvestable in year 31 favours the trend-stationary reading used by the G camp. Under that reading B,C,D,F are false, A,E,H are false as stated, and the strict expected-value ordering G is the strongest true statement in the list. reflection_text.3:
The core dispute is mean-equivalence on a fixed date vs a mean-increasing timing premium in the 31st-year liquidation window.

Basket A is degenerate: P_A(t)=P0 1.10^t, E[V_A]=P0 1.10^31, liquidation option worth zero. Basket B has the same 10% p.a. arithmetic mean growth, E[P_B(t)]=P0 1.10^t = E[P_A(t)], so up to the forced 30-year hold the two baskets are mean-equivalent.

The 31st year is an American sell / adaptive liquidation window. In the trend-stationary reading that the wording “constant autocovariance”, “random walk around a mean with drift” and linear 10% trend evokes,
P_B(t)=m(t)+X_t, m(t)=P0 1.10^t, E[X_t]=0, X stationary with constant variance.
Then E[P_B(t)|F_s]=P_B(s)+m(t)-m(s)+(ρ^{t-s}-1)X_s with ρ<1, i.e. the detrended component is mean-reverting. Conditional on F_t the one-step expected increment is m(t+Δ)-m(t)+(ρ^{Δ}-1)X_t, so for X_t>0 the conditional mean is lower than the trend increment and it is optimal to sell more aggressively on up-excursions and hold on down-excursions. 

With an adapted liquidation rate α_t, α30=0, α31=1,
E[V_B]=∫ m(t)dα_t + E[∫ X_t dα_t] > ∫ m(t)dα_t = m(31) up to negligible drift terms, because dα_t can be made positively correlated with X_t. In the stopping limit E[V_B*]→ E[sup_{30≤t≤31} P_B(t)] = m(31)+E[max X_t] > m(31)=E[P_B(31)]. The E[max X_t]>0 is the usual look-back/American premium, strictly increasing in weekly 20% volatility and zero for A.

Hence in expectation the optimally liquidated B dominates the deterministic A: E[V_B^opt]>E[V_A^opt]=P0 1.10^31. The dominance is only in expectation; a realisation of B can still finish below the certain A path, so E and H are false and A is the reverse ordering.

Martingale claims B,C,D,F are false: both price processes have a 10% drift, so P_t is a strict sub-martingale, not a martingale. A is deterministic and not a martingale. The stationary-returns argument that de-meaning the drift makes X_t a martingale and therefore E[∫ P_t dα_t] is drift-only is the stationary-returns fallacy; it ignores the correlation E[X_t dα_t] that an adapted policy can create and the fact that P_t=m(t)X_t is not a martingale.

Majority of colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 argue for G. Minority 10,7 argue for C, i.e. same unconditional mean and no first-moment gain from timing, invoking optional sampling for the de-trended martingale X_t and claiming E[∫ P_t dα_t]=E[X30]E[∫ m(t)dα_t]. The disagreement hinges on whether the model is taken as geometric multiplicative martingale X_t=P_t/m(t) with optimal all-or-nothing stopping at T, or trend-stationary additive X_t with positively correlated liquidation. The problem’s constant autocovariance + “random walk around a mean with drift” phrasing supports the trend-stationary / mean-reverting interpretation used for G.

Unresolved nuance: exact magnitude depends on additive vs multiplicative specification and on the precise admissible liquidation set; the strongest statement that can be made from the given list is the strict expected-value ordering G. I am leaning to G as the most specific true statement, with C representing the fixed-date mean-equivalence view.
reflection_text.6:
The set-up remains A deterministic 10%/yr, $P_A(t)=P_0 1.10^{t}$; B has the same 10%/yr mean drift $E[P_B(t)]=P_0 1.10^{t}$ with non-degenerate stationary returns, ~20% weekly moves, constant long-run volatility. 30 years forced hold, 31st year free disposal with any adapted liquidation schedule $\alpha_{30}=0,\alpha_{31}=1$ and $V=\int_{30}^{31}P_t d\alpha_t$. 

First-moment equivalence on fixed dates is agreed: $E[P_B(t)]=P_A(t)$. Hence up to $t=30$ the two baskets are mean equivalent. The whole dispute is the value of the 31st-year American / timing option.

* Pro-G camp 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9: $P_B(t)=m(t)+X_t$ or $m(t)X_t$ with $m(t)=P_0 1.10^{t}$ and $E[X_t]=0$, $E[X_t|F_s]=X_s$. $P_B$ is a strict sub-martingale with 10% drift, not a martingale. The liquidation value is $V_B =\int m(t)X_t d\alpha_t$. By choosing $d\alpha_t$ positively correlated with $X_t$ – sell more when the price is on an up excursion, hold when down – the term $E[\int X_t d\alpha_t]$ can be made $>0$. In the limit $E[V_B^{\rm opt}] \to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_B(t)] =m(31)+E[\max X_t] >m(31)$. Hence $E[V_B^{\rm opt}]>E[V_A]=P_0 1.10^{31}$. The premium is the classic look-back/American sell value created by $\sigma>0$; it is strictly increasing in volatility and zero for A. Dominance is in expectation only: realisations of B can finish below A, so pathwise statements E and H are false. Martingale/stationary-return claims B,C,D,F are false because price processes have a 10% drift; A is deterministic and not a martingale; demeaned returns are a martingale but prices are not.

* Anti-G camp 10,7: stationary return law with mean 10% implies after de-meaning $X_t=P_t/1.10^{t}$ is a martingale. The liquidation value is $V_B=\int 1.10^{t}X_t d\alpha_t$ and, via optional sampling, $E[X_\tau]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping $\tau$. Linearity then gives $E[V_B|F_{30}]=X_{30}E[\int1.10^{t}d\alpha_t]$, so the mean depends only on the mean growth factor, not on volatility. The option to time liquidation is a mean-preserving spread; $E[\max P_t]>E[P_T]$ concerns the distribution of the running maximum, not the mean of an admissible liquidation of the whole position. Hence unconditional expected liquidation is $P_0 1.10^{31}$ for both, i.e. C.

The key disagreement is attainability of the $\sup$ premium with a full liquidation constraint and the covariance $Cov(1.10^{\tau},X_\tau)$. G camp argues the optimal adapted $\alpha_t$ can be made positively correlated with $X_t$, yielding $E[m(\tau)X_\tau]>E[m(\tau)]E[X_{30}]$, and the familiar American sell value is strictly positive for $\sigma>0$. 10/7 reply that for a martingale $E[\int X d\alpha]=0$ for predictable finite-variation $\alpha$, so the covariance is washed out and the first moment cannot be created.

Evidence retained: colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 converge on G with the Snell envelope / max $X$ argument; colleagues 7,10,8 remark note mean equivalence on fixed dates. The stationary-returns fallacy is repeatedly identified: stationary returns with non-zero mean give a sub-martingale price, not a martingale.

Current belief unchanged: the 31st-year free disposal creates a strictly positive volatility / timing premium in expectation. The strongest true statement in the list is the strict expected-value ordering $E[\text{liquidation}|B] > E[\text{liquidation}|A]$, i.e. G. A is reverse, B,C,D,F are false on their premises, E and H are false because dominance is not pathwise. Unresolved formal nuance is whether the gradual liquidation constraint fully allows approaching $E[\sup P]$; all G arguments assume it does, which is the standard American-option intuition.

reflection_text.1:
After round 1 the core facts are stable. Both baskets have the same 10 % p.a. arithmetic drift in mean so on any fixed calendar date E[P_B(t)]=E[P_A(t)]=P0 1.10^t. Basket A is degenerate P_A(t)=P0 1.10^t and the 31st-year liquidation option is worthless, V_A*=P0 1.10^31 with probability one.

Basket B is trend-stationary in the intended reading P_B(t)=m(t)+X_t with m(t)=P0 1.10^t, E[X_t]=0, X stationary with constant second order and ≈20 % weekly moves. The first 30 years are forced hold so the pre-liquidation mean at 30 is mean-equivalent. The difference is the 31st year. With an adapted liquidation schedule α_t ↑1 on [30,31]

V_B=∫_{30}^{31}P_B(t) dα_t =∫ m(t)dα_t +∫ X_t dα_t.

The deterministic part integrates to m(31) up to negligible dt. The stochastic part can be made positive in expectation by making dα_t positively correlated with X_t – sell more aggressively on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions – and the control is forced to α_31=1. Hence

E[V_B^{opt}] = m(31)+E[∫ X_t dα_t^*] > m(31)=E[P_B(31)]

and in the limit E[V_B^{opt}] → E[max_{30≤t≤31}P_B(t)] = m(31)+E[max_{30≤t≤31}X_t] > m(31). The E[max X]>0 is the usual American/look-back value created by the 20% weekly volatility, zero for A.

Hence in expectation E[V_B^{opt}] > E[V_A^{opt}] =P0 1.10^31. The dominance is only in expectation; a realisation of B can finish below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false. Both price processes have a 10% drift, P_A degenerate, P_B a strict sub-martingale in prices, so B,C,D,F are false on their premises. Stationary one-period returns do not make prices martingales and do not preclude a first-moment gain from adapted exercise.

The current round is split. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 hold G and give the same trend-stationary + adapted-sale / Snell envelope argument, with the strict inequality E[sup P_B]>E[P_B(31)]. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue for C, stressing stationary returns, the martingale property of the de-trended price X_t^B=P_t^B/1.10^t, optional sampling E[X_τ]=E[X_30], and that the mean of an adapted liquidation of the whole position is linear in the drift only, so the 20% moves only create a mean-preserving spread. They claim the max is not attainable by a single self-financing liquidation and that timing cannot create first-moment alpha.

The disagreement is whether the positive correlation between the adapted liquidation rate and the stationary excursions can be exploited to raise the unconditional first moment. The G camp treats the 31st year as an American sell window with a strictly positive look-back premium; the C camp treats it as an averaging problem where optional stopping for the de-trended martingale cancels the first-moment gain. Under the trend-stationary, constant-volatility specification given in the problem the American premium is the intended effect, and the strongest true statement on the list remains the strict expected-value dominance of the optimally liquidated volatile basket, i.e. G, with A the reverse ordering and all martingale/same-mean statements false.
reflection_text.9:
The discussion is now split between a volatility-timing / look-back premium view and a stationary-returns / optional-sampling view.

Basket A is deterministic, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and under any admissible liquidation in year 31 $V^{A}_{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ with zero option value.

Basket B can be written in trend-stationary / trend-martingale form
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}=m(t)X_{t}$ with $m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and
$E[X_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=X_{s}$, $E[X_{t}]=1$.
Hence $E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ on every fixed calendar date and
$P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the same 10% drift, not a martingale.
The first 30 years are forced, so the pre-liquidation means coincide.

The 31st year is an American sell window.  For an adapted liquidation rate
$\alpha_{t}$ with $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$ the cash obtained is
$V_{B}(\alpha)=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}(-d\alpha_{t})$.  Write the two-period
discrete proxy: with $a_{1}=a_{1}(X_{1})$ the fraction sold at $t=1$,

$E[a_{1}P_{1}+(1-a_{1})P_{2}\mid\mathcal F_{1}]
 =X_{1}\big[m_{2}-a_{1}(m_{2}-m_{1})\big]$

and $E[P_{2}\mid\mathcal F_{1}]=(m_{2}/m_{1})P_{1}>P_{1}$ because $m$ is
strictly increasing.  Hence

$E[a_{1}(P_{1}-P_{2})\mid\mathcal F_{1}]\le0$

with strict inequality for $a_{1}>0$.  In continuous time
$E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]
\le E[P^{B}_{31}]$, equality only for the buy-and-hold rule $\alpha_{t}\equiv1$
on $[30,31]$.  The classic $E[\max_{t}P_{t}]>E[P_{T}]$ inequality is true for
the pathwise maximum, but the time of the maximum is not an $\mathcal F_{t}$-
stopping time; the sup is not attainable by an adapted sale schedule, and
optional sampling for the de-trended martingale $X_{t}=P^{B}_{t}/m(t)$ gives
$E[X_{\tau}]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping time.  The correlation that
would make $d\alpha_{t}$ positively correlated with $X_{t}$ is exactly
offset by the foregone deterministic drift $dm(t)>0$.

Hence under any admissible, non-reinvesting liquidation policy
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]\le E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{*}]$, and the
optimal policy in expectation is to hold to the end of the 31st year.
The $20\%$ weekly volatility therefore creates a mean-preserving spread and
a positive look-back value in the distribution, $E[\sup P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$,
but it does not create a first-moment gain that can be realised by an
adapted liquidation schedule.

That makes the expected-value ranking $E[V^{B}]>E[V^{A}]$ in G unattainable
and the pathwise necessary dominances E and H false.  The deterministic
basket A is not a martingale and neither is B; the price processes are
strict sub-martingales with identical 10% drift, so B,C,D,F are false on the
literal martingale wording, but the stationary one-period return law does
imply identical first moments and identical average returns for the two
strategies.  The strongest true statement available on the list is the
equality of first moments / average returns, essentially the stationary-
return statement C, with B being the same claim at the level of average
return.  The earlier G belief relied on the unattainable sup/look-back
value; the optional-sampling / drift-dominated argument of Colleagues 10
and 7 removes the mean gain.

Unresolved nuance: the statement phrases “both options are martingales”
is sloppy – the de-trended returns are martingale differences and the
prices are sub-martingales – but the conclusion of equal expected
liquidation value and equal average return holds.  A and E remain false by
reversal, H remains false pathwise.

5.text:
Basket A is degenerate

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s., so for every admissible liquidation
$\alpha_{t}\uparrow1$ on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{A}_{t}d\alpha_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$

with probability one. The 31st year option is worth zero.

Write B in trend stationary form as the statement invites

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t},\qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\;E[X_{t}]=0,$

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ and $X_{t}$ is stationary with constant
variance, $E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t},\;|\rho|<1$.
After de-meaning the drift $X_{t}$ is mean reverting, $P^{B}_{t}$ is a
strict sub-martingale with the same $10\%$ p.a. arithmetic drift as A.
On a fixed calendar date the two baskets are mean equivalent and the
first 30 years of forced holding are the same in expectation. The
difference is the American sell window $[30,31]$.

With an adapted liquidation rate $\alpha_{t}$,

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
      =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+ \int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.

The first term is $m(31)$ up to $O(\Delta t)$.  $d\alpha_{t}$ can be
chosen positively correlated with $X_{t}$: sell more when the price is
on an up excursion relative to trend and hold when it is down. With
$\alpha_{31}=1$ this is the usual American/look-back value

$E\!\left[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}\right]\ge
E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
= m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]>m(31)$.

For a non-degenerate stationary $X$, $\max X>0$ a.s. and
$E[\max X]> \max E[X]=0$ by convexity.  In the geometric reading
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)X_{t}$ with $E[X_{t+1}|{\cal F}_{t}]=X_{t}$, 
$E[P^{B}_{\tau}]=E[1.10^{\tau}X_{\tau}] >1.10^{31}E[X_{31}]$ for a
$\tau$ positively correlated with $X_{\tau}$.  In either reading the
$20\%$ weekly volatility creates a strictly positive timing premium in
the 31st year, which is zero for the deterministic A.

Hence

$E\!\left[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}\right] > P_{0}1.10^{31}
 =E\!\left[V^{A}\right]=V^{A}$,

i.e. the optimally liquidated volatile basket dominates the deterministic
basket in expectation. The dominance is only in expectation: on a given
realisation $P^{B}_{31}$ can lie below $P^{A}_{31}$, so the pathwise
statements E and H are false.

The price processes are not martingales. $P^{A}$ is deterministic and
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale with $10\%$ drift.
Stationary one-period returns with a non-zero drift do not make prices
martingales. B,C,D,F are therefore false and A is the reverse of the true
ordering.

The strongest true statement on the list is the strict expected-value
dominance of the optimally timed B liquidation,

$E[\,\text{liquidation}|B\,]>E[\,\text{liquidation}|A\,]$,

i.e. G.

2.text:
Basket A is degenerate

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$,

so for any admissible liquidation $\alpha_{t}\uparrow1$ on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}\equiv\int_{30}^{31}P^{A}_{t}d\alpha_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$

deterministically and the 31st-year timing option is worthless.

Write B in trend stationary form.  With a 10% p.a. linear trend and
constant autocovariance

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t},\qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\;E[X_{t}]=0,$

or $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)X_{t}$ with $E[X_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=X_{s}$, 
$E[X_{t}]=1$. Hence on a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=P^{A}_{t}$,

so the forced 30 yr hold is mean-equivalent.  The price processes are
strict sub-martingales with the common 10% drift; $A$ is not a martingale
and $B$ is not a martingale in prices. B,C,D,F are therefore false.

In year 31 the trader can choose an adapted liquidation rate
$\alpha_{t},\;\alpha_{30}=0,\alpha_{31}=1$.  Then

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
               =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.

The second term can be made strictly positive in expectation by making
$d\alpha_{t}$ positively correlated with the stationary noise $X_{t}$:
sell more when $P^{B}_{t}$ is on an up excursion relative to trend and
hold when it is down.  With $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]
   =\rho^{\Delta}X_{t},\;|\rho|<1$,

$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]-P^{B}_{t}
      =m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t},$

so the conditional mean is depressed after an up move.  The attainable
value tends to the Snell envelope

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]
   \approx E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
   =m(31)+E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
   >m(31).$

Hence

$E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
   =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]
   >m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}]$,

the usual American / look-back premium generated by the 20% weekly
volatility.  With optimal adapted liquidation

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A\,{\rm opt}}]=V^{A}$.

The dominance is in expectation only: a realisation of B can finish
below the deterministic A path, so the necessarily statements E and H
are false.  The strongest true statement on the list is the strict
expected-value ordering

$E[\text{liquidation}\mid B]>E[\text{liquidation}\mid A]$,

i.e. G.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the stationary-return / de-trended martingale point is the one that survives once you write the liquidation value correctly.

Write the two baskets with the common 10% arithmetic drift removed:

$X_{t}^{A}=P_{t}^{A}/1.10^{t}=P_{0}$, $X_{t}^{B}=P_{t}^{B}/1.10^{t}$ with 
$E[X_{t+Δ}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]=X_{t}$ and $E[X_{t}^{B}]=P_{0}$.

So after de-meaning the drift the two baskets are martingale-equivalent: $X^{A}$ degenerate, $X^{B}$ a true martingale. In prices

$E[P_{t}^{B}]=1.10^{t}E[X_{t}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}=P_{t}^{A}=E[P_{t}^{A}]$

on every fixed calendar date. The first 30 years are a forced hold, so the mean wealth at $t=30$ is identical.

In the 31st year any admissible liquidation is an adapted, non-decreasing
$\alpha_{t}$ with $\alpha_{30}=0$, $\alpha_{31}=1$ and

$V^{B}= \int_{30}^{31}P_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}
      =\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}$.

Conditional on $\mathcal F_{30}$ the martingale property of $X^{B}$ gives

$E\!\left[V^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\; X_{30}^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =X_{30}^{B}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right],$

and the same expression holds for the degenerate basket with $X^{A}\equiv P_{0}$.
The first-moment contribution therefore depends only on the mean
growth factor $\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}$ and on $X_{30}$, not on the
volatility of $X^{B}$. The best you can do in expectation is to reproduce the
fixed-horizon mean $P_{0}1.10^{31}$; any adaptation of $d\alpha_{t}$ to the
noise $X_{t}$ is a mean-preserving re-weighting of a martingale.

The $E[\max P_{t}]>E[P_{T}]$ statements quoted for G are statements about the
distribution of the running maximum, not about $E[\int P_{t}d\alpha_{t}]$
under an admissible liquidation of the whole position. $E[\max X_{t}]>0$ is
true for a non-degenerate stationary noise, but the maximum is not
attainable by a single adapted liquidation schedule that must liquidate the
entire holding to zero by $t=31$. With proportional liquidation the
up-crossings are averaged with the down-crossings and optional sampling for
the detrended martingale $X_{t}$ gives $E[X_{\tau}]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded
stopping time $\tau$, i.e. no first-moment alpha can be created by timing.

Hence the 20% weekly moves in B only create a spread around the common 10%
arithmetic drift that A attains deterministically. Unconditionally

$E[V^{B\;{\rm opt}}]=E[V^{A\;{\rm opt}}]=P_{0}1.10^{31},$

the two strategies have the same average return and the same expected
liquidation value. The volatility is a risk effect, not a mean effect.
That is the stationary-return martingale intuition captured by C.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with 7 and 10 on the first-moment point.

Write the de-trended price $X_t^B = P_t^B / 1.10^{\,t}$ and $X_t^A = P_0$.
By construction $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=X_t$, so after removing the common 10% arithmetic drift the two baskets are martingale equivalent: $X_t^B$ is a true martingale and $X_t^A$ is the degenerate martingale $X_t^A\equiv P_0$.
In prices

$P_t^B =1.10^{\,t}X_t^B$, $E[P_t^B\mid\mathcal F_s]=P_s^B 1.10^{\,t-s}$,

so $P_t^B$ and $P_t^A$ are strict sub-martingales with the same drift, and on any fixed calendar date

$E[P_t^B]=P_0 1.10^{\,t}=P_t^A$.

The first 30 years are forced hold, so the mean at $t=30$ is identical.

The 31st year is a liquidation window with an adapted, non-decreasing $\alpha_t$, $\alpha_{30}=0$, $\alpha_{31}=1$,

$V_B =\int_{30}^{31} P_t^B d\alpha_t =\int_{30}^{31} 1.10^{\,t}X_t^B d\alpha_t$.

For any predictable $\alpha$, $E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t}X_t^B d\alpha_t\mid\mathcal F_{30}\big]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$

by the martingale property of $X_t^B$. The same expression holds for A with $X_t^A\equiv P_0$. Hence

$E[V_B\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=X_{30}^B\,E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$,
$E[V_A\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=P_0\,E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$,

and unconditionally $E[V_B]=E[V_A]=P_0 1.10^{31}$ up to the negligible deterministic $O(\Delta t)$ from the drift weighting inside the integral.

The $E[\sup P_t]>E[P_T]$ that is repeatedly quoted for G is a statement about the distribution of the running maximum, not about the mean of an admissible complete liquidation. The maximum is not attainable by a single liquidation of the whole position with $\alpha_{31}=1$. With a proportional liquidation constraint the up-crossings are averaged out with the down-crossings; the expectation of the integral is linear in $E[P_t]$. Optional stopping for the de-trended martingale $X_t^B$ gives $E[X_\tau]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping time $\tau\in[30,31]$, so the drift-removed first moment cannot be created by timing.

In particular 8 itself notes “on a strict risk-neutral unconditional mean the two unconditional terminal means coincide, $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$”. The volatility in B only creates a mean-preserving spread around the common 10% arithmetic drift. Stationary one-period returns with a non-zero mean do not create first-moment alpha from an adapted liquidation of the entire holding; they create dispersion.

Hence the mean liquidation value is the same for the deterministic and the volatile basket. That is the stationary-returns/martingale-after-de-meaning intuition: same average return, same expected value.

3.text:
Basket A is degenerate

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ , $V^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s. and the 31st year
liquidation option is worthless.

Write B in the trend-stationary form that the wording
`constant autocovariance / linear 10% trend / random walk around a mean
with drift` is intended to evoke,

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t},\qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\quad E[X_{t}]=0,$

$X_{t}$ stationary with constant variance and $E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]
=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$, $|\rho|<1$.  Hence on any fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,

so the forced 30 year hold is mean-equivalent. The first moment
difference is created in the free disposal window $[30,31]$.

Let $\alpha_{t}$ be an adapted liquidation rate, $\alpha_{30}=0$,
$\alpha_{31}=1$. Then

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
           =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.

The first term is $m(31)$ up to $O(\Delta t)$. The second term can be made
strictly positive in expectation by making $d\alpha_{t}$ positively
correlated with the current stationary noise $X_{t}$: sell faster on up
excursions $X_{t}>0$ and hold on down excursions $X_{t}<0$.  In the limit

$E[V^{B*}]\to E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
        =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]
        >m(31)$,

because $\max X_{t}$ is convex and $E[\max X_{t}]> \max E[X_{t}]=0$ for any
non-degenerate stationary $X$. The $E[\max X_{t}]>0$ is the usual
American/look-back premium created by the $20\%$ weekly volatility; it is
zero for the deterministic A.

Hence with optimal adapted liquidation in year 31

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha^{*}_{t}\right]
>m(31)=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$,

i.e. $E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>E[V^{A\,{\rm opt}}]$. The dominance is in
expectation only: a realisation of B can finish below the certain A path,
so the necessarily/pathwise statements E and H are false.

The price processes are not martingales. $P^{A}$ is deterministic and
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the 10% drift.
Stationarity of the one-period return law does not make $P_{t}$ a
martingale and does not preclude a first-moment gain from adapted
exercise. The de-meaned martingale $X_{t}$ argument of colleagues 10 and 7
gives mean equivalence on a fixed calendar date, $E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]$,
which is true, but it ignores the $E[X_{t}d\alpha_{t}]$ term that an
optimal liquidation policy can create. That is the stationary-returns
fallacy.

The strongest true statement on the list is the strict expected-value
dominance of the optimally liquidated volatile basket,

$E[\text{liquidation}|B]>E[\text{liquidation}|A]$,

i.e. G. A is the reverse ordering and the martingale/equality
statements B,C,D,F are false.

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ so that with a liquidation schedule
$\alpha_{t}\uparrow 1$ on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}=\int_{30}^{31}P^{A}_{t}d\alpha_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ 

is deterministic and the 31st year option is worthless.

Write B in the trend stationary form implied by constant autocovariance
and a 10 % p.a. linear trend

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t},\qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\quad E[X_{t}]=0,$

$E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t},\;|\rho|<1$, so that

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ on any fixed calendar date. 
The 30 yr forced hold is therefore mean equivalent.

On $[30,31]$ let $0\le \alpha_{t}\le1$ be the adapted fraction still
held, $\alpha_{30}=1,\;\alpha_{31}=0$, and

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})
       =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d(-\alpha_{t}).$

Up to the $O(\Delta t)$ deterministic term 
$\int m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})=m(31)$.
Conditionally

$E\!\left[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\right]-P^{B}_{t}
   =m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t},$

so $E[\Delta P^{B}|{\cal F}_{t}]$ is depressed when $X_{t}>0$ and
enhanced when $X_{t}<0$.  Hence it is optimal to make $d(-\alpha_{t})$
positively correlated with $X_{t}$: sell faster on up excursions of the
stationary noise and hold on down excursions.  With an adapted
$\alpha^{*}$,

$E[V^{B}_{\alpha^{*}}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d(-\alpha^{*}_{t})\right]
   >m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}] .$

In the limit $E[V^{B}_{\alpha^{*}}]\to
E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
=m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]>m(31)$,

the usual American / look-back premium created by the non-degenerate
stationary noise, $20\%$ weekly, which is $0$ for A.  In particular

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{\rm opt}]=V^{A},$

i.e. $E[V^{B}] > E[V^{A}]$.  The dominance is in expectation only;
on a path $P^{B}_{31}$ can lie below the certain $P^{A}_{31}$, so E and H
are false.  

$P^{A}$ is degenerate and $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ is not a martingale,
it is a strict sub–martingale in the mean only.  The de-trended price
$P^{B}_{t}/1.10^{t}$ is not a martingale under the trend-stationary
specification, so the stationary-returns martingale claims B,C,D,F are
false and A is the reverse ordering.  The strongest true statement on
the list is the strict mean ordering in favour of the optimally
liquidated volatile basket.

8.text:
Basket A is degenerate

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ so that for any admissible liquidation
$\alpha_{t}\uparrow1$ on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{A}_{t}d\alpha_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s.
and the 31st-year timing option is worth zero.

Write B in trend stationary form $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ with
$m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and $E[X_{t}]=0$, $X_{t}$ stationary with
constant autocovariance, or equivalently $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)X_{t}$ with
$E[X_{t+dt}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=X_{t}$ and $E[X_{t}]=1$.  
Hence $E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ on any fixed calendar date and the
two baskets are mean equivalent up to $t=30$.  Both price processes have
a $10\%$ arithmetic drift, so $P^{A}$ is degenerate and $P^{B}$ is a
strict sub-martingale in prices; the de-trended component $X_{t}$ is the
martingale.  B,C,D,F are therefore false.

Let $\alpha_{t}$ be an adapted liquidation rate with $\alpha_{30}=0$,
$\alpha_{31}=1$.  With $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+ \int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.
The first term is $m(31)+o(1)$.  Because $d\alpha_{t}$ can be chosen
adapted, $E[\int X_{t}d\alpha_{t}]$ can be made $>0$ by making
$d\alpha_{t}$ positively correlated with the up-excursions of the
stationary noise.  In the two-date illustration with
$X_{1}=\rho X_{0}+\varepsilon$, $0<\rho<1$,

$E[V\mid{\cal F}_{0}]=m_{1}+(m_{0}-m_{1})f+X_{0}[\rho+f(1-\rho)]$,

so the optimal $f=f(X_{0})$ is $1$ iff $X_{0}>(m_{1}-m_{0})/(1-\rho)$,
i.e. sell more aggressively when the price is on an up excursion
relative to trend and hold when it is down.  In the continuous limit

$E[V^{B\,*}]\;\to\;E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]
     =m(31)+E\Big[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\Big]
     >m(31)$,

$E[\max X_{t}]>0$ for every non-degenerate stationary $X$.  This is the
usual American/look-back premium created by the $20\%$ weekly volatility
in year 31.  It is strictly positive for B and zero for A.

Hence with optimal adapted liquidation in the 31st year

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]=E\big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\big]
>m(31)=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A},$

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>E[V^{A\,{\rm opt}}]$

in expectation only.  A realisation of B can still finish below the
deterministic A path so the pathwise necessarily statements E and H are
false.  The stationary-return/martingale equality claims B,C,D,F are
false because the price processes carry the $10\%$ drift.  The strict
expected-value ordering in favour of the volatile basket is G.

6.text:

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$,

so with any admissible liquidation on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{A}_{t}d\alpha_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$

is certain and the 31st year option is worthless.

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}, \qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\;E[X_{t}]=0,$

with $X_{t}$ stationary, $\operatorname{Var}X_{t}>0$, constant long run
volatility and $E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$,
$|\rho|<1$.  On a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=P^{A}_{t}$,

so the first 30 years of forced holding are mean equivalent.  In the
31st year

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
 =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+ \int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}.$

$d\alpha_{t}$ can be made positively correlated with $X_{t}$: sell more
on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions.
For a non-degenerate stationary $X$ the Snell envelope is strictly above
the European value,

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
 =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]
 >m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}].$

$E[\max X_{t}]> \max E[X_{t}]=0$ is the usual American / look-back
value created by the $\approx20\%$ weekly volatility.  Hence with the
optimal adapted liquidation

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]
 =E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]
 >P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}=E[V^{A}].$

The dominance is in expectation only; a realisation of B can finish
below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false.  $P^{A}$ is
degenerate and $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale with
10 % arithmetic drift, so B,C,D,F are false and A is the reverse
ordering.  The strongest true statement on the list is the strict
expected value dominance of the optimally liquidated volatile basket,

$E[{\rm liquidation}|B]>E[{\rm liquidation}|A],$

Basket A is degenerate $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and with any admissible
liquidation in the $31$st year

$V^{A}_{*}\equiv P_{0}1.10^{31}$,
$E[V^{A}_{*}]=V^{A}_{*}$ and the 31st-year option value is $0$.

Write B in trend stationary form $P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$,
$m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}$, $E[X_{t}]=0$, $\operatorname{Var}X_{t}$ constant and
$E\!\left[X_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\right]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$,
$|\rho|<1$.  In particular $X_{t}$ is stationary with constant
autocovariance, mean-reverting around the $10\%$ arithmetic drift.
On a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=P^{A}_{t}$,

so the forced first $30$ years are mean equivalent.  The price process
itself is a strict sub-martingale with the $10\%$ drift, $A$ is
deterministic, $B,C,D,F$ are the stationary-returns fallacy.

Year $31$ is an American sell window. With an adapted liquidation rate
$\alpha_{t},\;\alpha_{30}=0,\;\alpha_{31}=1$,

$V^{B}_{\alpha}=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
   =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.

Conditional on ${\cal F}_{30}$ the second term can be made positive in
expectation by making $d\alpha_{t}$ positively correlated with $X_{t}$:
sell faster on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold when $X_{t}<0$.
With $E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$ the conditional
mean increment is

$E[P_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]-P_{t}=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t},$

so for $X_{t}>0$ the mean-reversion term depresses the conditional mean
and it is optimal to liquidate more aggressively, and vice-versa for
$X_{t}<0$.  Hence in closed form

$E[V^{B}_{*}|{\cal F}_{30}]
   \ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]
   =m(31)+E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]
   >m(31)$

because $\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}>0$ a.s. for a non-degenerate stationary
$X$ and $E[\max X]>0$ by convexity.  In the limit

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]=E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
   =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]
   >m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$.

The $20\%$ weekly volatility creates a strictly positive
American/look-back timing premium in the $31$st year which is zero for $A$.
The dominance is in expectation only: on a realisation $P^{B}_{31}$ can
finish below the deterministic $P^{A}_{31}$, so $E$ and $H$ are false and
the ordering is not pathwise. The stationary-return/martingale claims
$B,C,D,F$ are false because the price processes have a $10\%$ arithmetic
drift and are strict sub-martingales. The strict mean ordering is
$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>E[V^{A}]$, i.e. $G$ is the strongest true statement
in the list.

9.text:
The 30 yr forced hold is identical in mean for the two baskets.

Write the B price in de-trended form

P^B_t = m(t)+X_t ,   m(t)=P0 1.10^{t},  E[X_t]=0

with X_t stationary,  Cov[X_t,X_{t+s}]=γ(s) ,  Var X_t = const>0,
E[X_{t+Δ}|F_t]=ρ^{Δ}X_t ,  |ρ|<1 ,  and

E[P^B_t]=m(t)=P^A_t .

Hence on any fixed calendar date

E[P^B_t]=E[P^A_t]=P0 1.10^{t}

and the 30 yr forced position has the same mean for A and B.  After
de-meaning the common 10 % drift the return innovations are stationary
with zero mean; in prices the two processes are strict
sub-martingales with the same 10 % drift, the price processes are not
martingales and A is degenerate.  The martingale statement is the usual
stationary-returns wording for the de-trended price relatives

X^B_t:=P^B_t/m(t) ,   E[X^B_{t+Δ}|F_t]=X^B_t ,

so the first moment is generated only by the deterministic drift m(t).

Let α_t∈[0,1], α_30=1, α_31=0 be the adapted fraction still held in
the liquidation year and

V_B(α)=∫_{30}^{31}P^B_t d(-α_t)=U_0+∫_{30}^{31}α_t dU_t,
U_t=m(t)+X_t .

Then

E[V_B(α)|F_{30}]
 =U_{30}+E[∫_{30}^{31}α_t dm(t)|F_{30}]
  +E[∫_{30}^{31}α_t dX_t|F_{30}]
 =U_{30}+E[∫_{30}^{31}α_t dm(t)|F_{30}] ,

because X is a zero-mean stationary martingale-difference after
detrending and the stochastic integral has zero mean.  With dm(t)>0

U_{30}+∫_{30}^{31}α_t dm(t) ≤ U_{30}+∫_{30}^{31} dm(t)
      =m(31)+X_{30}+∫_{30}^{31}dm(t)-m(31) ?

In particular pointwise α_t≤1 and X_t>0 gives

V_B(α)=U_0+∫α_t dU_t ≤U_0+∫ dU_t =U_T

in expectation, and the drift term ∫α_t dm(t) is maximised in
expectation by α_t≡1 on [30,31].  Hence for every admissible adapted
liquidation

E[V_B(α)|F_{30}]≤E[P^B_{31}|F_{30}]
   =m(31)X^B_{30}=P^B_{30}1.10 ,

with equality only for the buy-and-hold liquidation α_t≡1, i.e. sell
all at the end of the 31st year.  The de-trended martingale optional
sampling gives E[X^B_τ]=E[X^B_{30}] for any bounded stopping time τ,
so the drift-removed first moment cannot be created by timing.

Hence

E[V^{B}_{opt}]=E[P^B_{31}]=P0 1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*} ,
E[V^{A}]=V^{A}_{*}=P0 1.10^{31} ,

i.e. the two strategies have the same unconditional mean and the same
average return.  The 20 % weekly volatility creates a mean-preserving
spread and E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t]>E[P^B_{31}], the usual
look-back/American value, but the sup is not attainable by an adapted
liquidation of the whole position; the up excursions are exactly
balanced by the down excursions and the deterministic drift dominates
the mean-reversion bias.  On any realisation B can finish below the
deterministic A path, so the pathwise dominances E and H are false and
the strict expected-value ordering G is not realisable.  The
stationary-return / de-meaned-martingale intuition is therefore the
only first-moment statement that survives, i.e. the equality of
expected liquidation value / average return, the statement in C, B
being the same claim at the level of average return.

      =\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}$.

$E\!\left[V^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\; X_{30}^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =X_{30}^{B}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right],$

and the same expression holds for the degenerate basket with $X^{A}\equiv P_{0}$.
The first-moment contribution therefore depends only on the mean
growth factor $\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}$ and on $X_{30}$, not on the
volatility of $X^{B}$. The best you can do in expectation is to reproduce the
fixed-horizon mean $P_{0}1.10^{31}$; any adaptation of $d\alpha_{t}$ to the
noise $X_{t}$ is a mean-preserving re-weighting of a martingale.

The $E[\max P_{t}]>E[P_{T}]$ statements quoted for G are statements about the
distribution of the running maximum, not about $E[\int P_{t}d\alpha_{t}]$
under an admissible liquidation of the whole position. $E[\max X_{t}]>0$ is
true for a non-degenerate stationary noise, but the maximum is not
attainable by a single adapted liquidation schedule that must liquidate the
entire holding to zero by $t=31$. With proportional liquidation the
up-crossings are averaged with the down-crossings and optional sampling for
the detrended martingale $X_{t}$ gives $E[X_{\tau}]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded
stopping time $\tau$, i.e. no first-moment alpha can be created by timing.

Hence the 20% weekly moves in B only create a spread around the common 10%
arithmetic drift that A attains deterministically. Unconditionally

$E[V^{B\;{\rm opt}}]=E[V^{A\;{\rm opt}}]=P_{0}1.10^{31},$

the two strategies have the same average return and the same expected
liquidation value. The volatility is a risk effect, not a mean effect.
That is the stationary-return martingale intuition captured by C.
public_text.10:
I’m with 7 and 10 on the first-moment point.

Write the de-trended price $X_t^B = P_t^B / 1.10^{\,t}$ and $X_t^A = P_0$.
By construction $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=X_t$, so after removing the common 10% arithmetic drift the two baskets are martingale equivalent: $X_t^B$ is a true martingale and $X_t^A$ is the degenerate martingale $X_t^A\equiv P_0$.
In prices

$P_t^B =1.10^{\,t}X_t^B$, $E[P_t^B\mid\mathcal F_s]=P_s^B 1.10^{\,t-s}$,

so $P_t^B$ and $P_t^A$ are strict sub-martingales with the same drift, and on any fixed calendar date

$E[P_t^B]=P_0 1.10^{\,t}=P_t^A$.

The first 30 years are forced hold, so the mean at $t=30$ is identical.

The 31st year is a liquidation window with an adapted, non-decreasing $\alpha_t$, $\alpha_{30}=0$, $\alpha_{31}=1$,

$V_B =\int_{30}^{31} P_t^B d\alpha_t =\int_{30}^{31} 1.10^{\,t}X_t^B d\alpha_t$.

For any predictable $\alpha$, $E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t}X_t^B d\alpha_t\mid\mathcal F_{30}\big]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$

by the martingale property of $X_t^B$. The same expression holds for A with $X_t^A\equiv P_0$. Hence

$E[V_B\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=X_{30}^B\,E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$,
$E[V_A\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=P_0\,E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{\,t} d\alpha_t\big]$,

and unconditionally $E[V_B]=E[V_A]=P_0 1.10^{31}$ up to the negligible deterministic $O(\Delta t)$ from the drift weighting inside the integral.

The $E[\sup P_t]>E[P_T]$ that is repeatedly quoted for G is a statement about the distribution of the running maximum, not about the mean of an admissible complete liquidation. The maximum is not attainable by a single liquidation of the whole position with $\alpha_{31}=1$. With a proportional liquidation constraint the up-crossings are averaged out with the down-crossings; the expectation of the integral is linear in $E[P_t]$. Optional stopping for the de-trended martingale $X_t^B$ gives $E[X_\tau]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping time $\tau\in[30,31]$, so the drift-removed first moment cannot be created by timing.

In particular 8 itself notes “on a strict risk-neutral unconditional mean the two unconditional terminal means coincide, $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$”. The volatility in B only creates a mean-preserving spread around the common 10% arithmetic drift. Stationary one-period returns with a non-zero mean do not create first-moment alpha from an adapted liquidation of the entire holding; they create dispersion.

Hence the mean liquidation value is the same for the deterministic and the volatile basket. That is the stationary-returns/martingale-after-de-meaning intuition: same average return, same expected value.

Basket A is degenerate

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ , $V^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s. and the 31st year
liquidation option is worthless.

Write B in the trend-stationary form that the wording
`constant autocovariance / linear 10% trend / random walk around a mean
with drift` is intended to evoke,

$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t},\qquad m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t},\quad E[X_{t}]=0,$

$X_{t}$ stationary with constant variance and $E[X_{t+\Delta}|{\cal F}_{t}]
=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$, $|\rho|<1$.  Hence on any fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=m(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,

so the forced 30 year hold is mean-equivalent. The first moment
difference is created in the free disposal window $[30,31]$.

Let $\alpha_{t}$ be an adapted liquidation rate, $\alpha_{30}=0$,
$\alpha_{31}=1$. Then

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}
           =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d\alpha_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha_{t}$.

The first term is $m(31)$ up to $O(\Delta t)$. The second term can be made
strictly positive in expectation by making $d\alpha_{t}$ positively
correlated with the current stationary noise $X_{t}$: sell faster on up
excursions $X_{t}>0$ and hold on down excursions $X_{t}<0$.  In the limit

$E[V^{B*}]\to E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
        =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]
        >m(31)$,

because $\max X_{t}$ is convex and $E[\max X_{t}]> \max E[X_{t}]=0$ for any
non-degenerate stationary $X$. The $E[\max X_{t}]>0$ is the usual
American/look-back premium created by the $20\%$ weekly volatility; it is
zero for the deterministic A.

Hence with optimal adapted liquidation in year 31

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d\alpha^{*}_{t}\right]
>m(31)=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$,

i.e. $E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>E[V^{A\,{\rm opt}}]$. The dominance is in
expectation only: a realisation of B can finish below the certain A path,
so the necessarily/pathwise statements E and H are false.

The price processes are not martingales. $P^{A}$ is deterministic and
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the 10% drift.
Stationarity of the one-period return law does not make $P_{t}$ a
martingale and does not preclude a first-moment gain from adapted
exercise. The de-meaned martingale $X_{t}$ argument of colleagues 10 and 7
gives mean equivalence on a fixed calendar date, $E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]$,
which is true, but it ignores the $E[X_{t}d\alpha_{t}]$ term that an
optimal liquidation policy can create. That is the stationary-returns
fallacy.

The strongest true statement on the list is the strict expected-value
dominance of the optimally liquidated volatile basket,

$E[\text{liquidation}|B]>E[\text{liquidation}|A]$,

i.e. G. A is the reverse ordering and the martingale/equality
statements B,C,D,F are false.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round 0 / round 2 split is between the multiplicative de-trended-martingale reading and the additive trend-stationary reading that the wording forces.

Basket A is degenerate, $P^{A}_t=P_0 1.10^{t}$, $V^{A}=P_0 1.10^{31}$ a.s., 31st-year option value zero.

The text for B is “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10 % p.a. … high variance … random walk around a mean with drift … volatility constant over time”.  That is trend-stationary, not a geometric random walk with drift.  In the natural parametrisation

$P^{B}_t=m(t)+X_t,\qquad m(t)=P_0 1.10^{t},\;E[X_t]=0,$

$X_t$ stationary with constant variance/autocovariance, $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=\rho^{\Delta}X_t$, $|\rho|<1$.  Hence on any fixed calendar date $E[P^{B}_t]=m(t)=P^{A}_t$, so the forced 30-yr hold is mean-equivalent.  $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale in the arithmetic mean sense, not a price martingale, and $P^{A}$ is not a martingale.  B,C,D,F are false on the literal martingale wording.

In the free disposal window $[30,31]$ with an adapted liquidation rate $\alpha_t$, $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$,

$V^{B}_\alpha=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_t d(-\alpha_t)=\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d(-\alpha_t)+\int_{30}^{31}X_t d(-\alpha_t)$.

$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]-P^{B}_t=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_t$, so the conditional mean increment is depressed after an up excursion $X_t>0$ and enhanced after a down excursion.  It is therefore optimal to make $d(-\alpha_t)$ positively correlated with $X_t$: sell faster on up excursions relative to trend and hold on down excursions.  With an adapted $\alpha^*$,

$E[V^{B}_{\alpha^*}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_t d(-\alpha^*_t)\right]>m(31)$,

and in the limit $E[V^{B}_{opt}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_t]=m(31)+E[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_t]>m(31)$.

The $20\%$ weekly volatility creates a strictly positive American / look-back timing premium in the 31st year which is zero for A.  Hence

$E[V^{B}_{opt}]>P_0 1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$,

i.e. the optimally liquidated volatile basket strictly dominates the deterministic basket in expectation.  The dominance is in expectation only: on a path $P^{B}_{31}$ can lie below $P^{A}_{31}$, so the pathwise necessary statements E and H are false.  The $E[\sup P]>E[P_T]$ inequality is realisable with an adapted complete liquidation because the stationary noise is mean-reverting; the optional-sampling argument for the de-trended martingale $X_t=P_t/m(t)$ does not apply under the additive constant-autocovariance specification, and the $E[\int P_t d\alpha_t]$ mean is not invariant to the correlation between $d\alpha_t$ and $X_t$.

The stationary-return / de-meaned-martingale equality $E[V^{B}]=E[V^{A}]$ that Colleagues 7,10,9 push would hold under the multiplicative model $P^B_t=m(t)X_t$, $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=X_t$, which gives $E[aP_1+(1-a)P_2\mid\mathcal F_1]=P_1[a+(1-a)r]$ decreasing in $a$.  That model is inconsistent with the stated constant autocovariance and constant volatility.  Under the stated trend-stationary additive model the mean gain from timing is genuine.

Strongest true statement on the list is therefore the strict expected-value ordering in favour of the optimally liquidated B,

$E[\text{liquidation}|B]>E[\text{liquidation}|A]$,

i.e. G.  A is the reverse ordering, E and H are false pathwise, and B,C,D,F are false on martingale wording; C is the equality that would hold under the multiplicative martingale reading but not under the constant-autocovariance trend-stationary reading implied by the question.

Mean equivalence on fixed dates is agreed: $E[P_B(t)]=P_A(t)$. Price processes are strict sub-martingales with 10% drift, $A$ degenerate, not a martingale. Stationary-return/martingale statements B,C,D,F are false on the price level; de-trended $X_t^B=P_B(t)/1.10^{t}$ is a martingale.

Pro-G camp 1,2,3,4,5,6,8: Write $P_B(t)=m(t)+X_t$, $m(t)=P_0 1.10^{t}$, $E[X_t]=0$, $E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_t]=\rho^{\Delta}X_t$. Then
$V_B=\int m d(-\alpha)+\int X d(-\alpha)$, the first term = $m(31)$ up to $o(dt)$.
Because $E[P_{t+\Delta}|F_t]-P_t = m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_t$, conditional mean is depressed after an up move $X_t>0$. It is therefore optimal to make $d(-\alpha_t)$ positively correlated with $X_t$: sell faster on up excursions, hold on down excursions. In the limit $E[V_B^*]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_B(t)]=m(31)+E[\max X_t]>m(31)$. The $E[\max X_t]>0$ is the usual American/look-back premium, strictly increasing in volatility and zero for A. Anti-G camp 7,10 and now 9: De-trend $X_t^B=P_B(t)/1.10^{t}$. $E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_t]=X_t$, so $X_t^B$ is a true martingale. $V_B=\int 1.10^{t}X_t d\alpha_t$ and for predictable $\alpha$, $E[\int 1.10^{t}X_t d\alpha_t|F_{30}]=X_{30}E[\int1.10^{t}d\alpha_t]$. Optional sampling gives $E[X_\tau]=E[X_{30}]$ for any bounded stopping $\tau$. Hence $E[V_B]=E[V_A]=P_0 1.10^{31}$ unconditionally. $E[\sup P_t]>E[P_T]$ is about the distribution of the running maximum, not the mean of an admissible complete liquidation; with proportional liquidation up-crossings are averaged with down-crossings and the first moment cannot be created. Volatility is mean-preserving spread.

Key disagreement persists: attainability of the $\sup$ premium under the full-liquidation constraint and whether $E[\int X d\alpha]$ can be made $>0$ with predictable finite-variation $\alpha$. Colleague 8 gives a two-date illustration showing an optimal $f(X_0)$ that sells more when $X_0$ is high, and notes remark “on a strict risk-neutral unconditional mean the two unconditional terminal means coincide”. Colleague 9 now explicitly argues optional sampling kills the first-moment gain and concludes equality C.

A is reverse, B,C,D,F are false on their premises, E and H are false pathwise. reflection_text.9:
The round 0 / round 2 split is between the multiplicative de-trended-martingale reading and the additive trend-stationary reading that the wording forces.

Basket A is degenerate, $P^{A}_t=P_0 1.10^{t}$, $V^{A}=P_0 1.10^{31}$ a.s., 31st-year option value zero.

The text for B is “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10 % p.a. … high variance … random walk around a mean with drift … volatility constant over time”.  That is trend-stationary, not a geometric random walk with drift.  In the natural parametrisation

$P^{B}_t=m(t)+X_t,\qquad m(t)=P_0 1.10^{t},\;E[X_t]=0,$

$X_t$ stationary with constant variance/autocovariance, $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=\rho^{\Delta}X_t$, $|\rho|<1$.  Hence on any fixed calendar date $E[P^{B}_t]=m(t)=P^{A}_t$, so the forced 30-yr hold is mean-equivalent.  $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale in the arithmetic mean sense, not a price martingale, and $P^{A}$ is not a martingale.  B,C,D,F are false on the literal martingale wording.

In the free disposal window $[30,31]$ with an adapted liquidation rate $\alpha_t$, $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$,

$V^{B}_\alpha=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_t d(-\alpha_t)=\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d(-\alpha_t)+\int_{30}^{31}X_t d(-\alpha_t)$.

$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]-P^{B}_t=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_t$, so the conditional mean increment is depressed after an up excursion $X_t>0$ and enhanced after a down excursion.  It is therefore optimal to make $d(-\alpha_t)$ positively correlated with $X_t$: sell faster on up excursions relative to trend and hold on down excursions.  With an adapted $\alpha^*$,

$E[V^{B}_{\alpha^*}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_t d(-\alpha^*_t)\right]>m(31)$,

and in the limit $E[V^{B}_{opt}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_t]=m(31)+E[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_t]>m(31)$.

The $20\%$ weekly volatility creates a strictly positive American / look-back timing premium in the 31st year which is zero for A.  Hence

$E[V^{B}_{opt}]>P_0 1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$,

i.e. the optimally liquidated volatile basket strictly dominates the deterministic basket in expectation.  The dominance is in expectation only: on a path $P^{B}_{31}$ can lie below $P^{A}_{31}$, so the pathwise necessary statements E and H are false.  The $E[\sup P]>E[P_T]$ inequality is realisable with an adapted complete liquidation because the stationary noise is mean-reverting; the optional-sampling argument for the de-trended martingale $X_t=P_t/m(t)$ does not apply under the additive constant-autocovariance specification, and the $E[\int P_t d\alpha_t]$ mean is not invariant to the correlation between $d\alpha_t$ and $X_t$.

The stationary-return / de-meaned-martingale equality $E[V^{B}]=E[V^{A}]$ that Colleagues 7,10,9 push would hold under the multiplicative model $P^B_t=m(t)X_t$, $E[X_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=X_t$, which gives $E[aP_1+(1-a)P_2\mid\mathcal F_1]=P_1[a+(1-a)r]$ decreasing in $a$.  That model is inconsistent with the stated constant autocovariance and constant volatility.  Under the stated trend-stationary additive model the mean gain from timing is genuine.

Strongest true statement on the list is therefore the strict expected-value ordering in favour of the optimally liquidated B,

$E[\text{liquidation}|B]>E[\text{liquidation}|A]$,

i.e. G.  A is the reverse ordering, E and H are false pathwise, and B,C,D,F are false on martingale wording; C is the equality that would hold under the multiplicative martingale reading but not under the constant-autocovariance trend-stationary reading implied by the question.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with 10, 7 and now 9 on the first moment.

Write the common 10% arithmetic drift out.  Put

$E[P_{t}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}=P_{t}^{A}$.

The first 30 years are forced hold, so the mean wealth at $t=30$ is
identical.  The 31st year is a complete liquidation with an adapted
non-decreasing $\alpha_{t}$, $\alpha_{30}=0$, $\alpha_{31}=1$,

$V_{B}= \int_{30}^{31}P_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}
     =\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}$.

separation

$E\!\left[V_{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =X_{30}^{B}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]$

and the same expression with the degenerate $X^{A}\equiv P_{0}$.
The first moment therefore depends only on the mean growth factor
$\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}$ and on $X_{30}$, not on the volatility of
$X^{B}$.  In particular

$E\!\left[V_{B}\right]=P_{0}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]
     =P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V_{A}]$

conditionally on $\mathcal F_{30}$.  Optional sampling for the
de-trended martingale $X^{B}$ gives $E[X_{\tau}^{B}]=E[X_{30}^{B}]$ for
any bounded stopping time $\tau\in[30,31]$, so no first-moment alpha can
be created by timing the de-trended component.

distribution of the running maximum, but the maximum is not attainable
by an admissible complete liquidation with $\alpha_{31}=1$.  With
proportional liquidation the up-crossings are averaged with the
down-crossings; the expectation of the stochastic integral is linear in

deterministically.

same average return, same expected liquidation value.  $P^{A}$ is
degenerate, $P^{B}_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale in prices, so the

the two unconditional terminal means coincide, $E[V^{A}]=E[V^{B}]$”, which

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I want to clarify why the first-moment gain is not attainable from a complete liquidation in year 31, even though $E[\sup P_t]>E[P_T]$ is true as a distributional statement.

Write the common 10% arithmetic drift out. Put
$P_t^A=m(t)$ with $m(t)=P_0 1.10^t$ and 
$P_t^B=m(t)+X_t$, $E[X_t]=0$, $X_t$ stationary with constant autocovariance.
After de-meaning the drift
$Y_t^B:=P_t^B/m(t)$ satisfies $E[Y_{t+\Delta}\mid {\cal F}_t]=Y_t$ up to the
$O(\Delta t)$ deterministic drift term, i.e. the one-period return law is
stationary with mean $10\%$ p.a. The de-trended price is the martingale
equivalent of the degenerate basket
$Y_t^A\equiv1$. In prices $E[P_t^B\mid{\cal F}_s]=P_s^B1.10^{t-s}$ and
$E[P_t^B]=m(t)=P_t^A$ on any fixed calendar date.

On $[30,31]$ let $\alpha_t$ be the adapted fraction still held,
$\alpha_{30}=1,\;\alpha_{31}=0$, with the admissible proceeds
$V_B(\alpha)=\int_{30}^{31}P_t^B d(-\alpha_t)$.
Integration by parts gives
$V_B=P_{30}^B+\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t dP_t^B$
and with $dP_t^B=m'(t)dt+dX_t$
$E[V_B\mid{\cal F}_{30}]
 =P_{30}^B+E\big[\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t m'(t)dt\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]
  +E\big[\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t dX_t\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]$.
For the stationary zero-mean $X_t$ the last term is a mean-zero
martingale-difference integral; conditionally its expectation is
$-\kappa E[\int\alpha_t X_t dt]$ which is exactly offset in first moment
by the loss $\int m'(t)dt$ incurred by selling before $31$.
Indeed for any predictable $\alpha$
$E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_t^B d\alpha_t\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t} d\alpha_t\big]$,
so the first moment depends only on the deterministic drift weight
$\int 1.10^{t} d\alpha_t$ and on $X_{30}^B$, not on the volatility of $X$.
Optional sampling for the de-trended martingale $Y_t^B$ gives
$E[Y_\tau^B\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=Y_{30}^B$ for any bounded stopping
$\tau\in[30,31]$, i.e. no first-moment alpha can be created by timing.

Hence
$E[V_B(\alpha)\mid{\cal F}_{30}]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t} d\alpha_t\big]$
and the same expression holds for A with $X_{30}^A\equiv P_0$.
Unconditionally
$E[V_B^{\rm opt}]=E[V_A^{\rm opt}]=P_0 1.10^{31}$.
The $20\%$ weekly moves in B create a mean-preserving spread around the
common $10\%$ arithmetic drift. $E[\max_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B]>E[P_{31}^B]$
is true for the distribution of the running maximum, but the maximum is
not attainable by a single adapted liquidation of the whole position with
$\alpha_{31}=0$. With proportional liquidation the up-crossings are
averaged out with the down-crossings and the expectation of the integral
is linear in $E[P_t]$.

That is the stationary-returns martingale-after-de-meaning intuition:
same average return, same expected liquidation value. The unconditional
terminal means coincide, as 8 itself notes, $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$, and the
volatility in B is risk, not first-moment alpha. This is the statement in
C, with B the same claim at the level of average return.

 =\int_{30}^{31}m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})+\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})$.

$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]-P^{B}_{t}
 =m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t},$

so the conditional mean is depressed after an up excursion $X_{t}>0$
and enhanced after a down excursion.  It is therefore optimal to make
$d(-\alpha_{t})$ positively correlated with $X_{t}$: sell faster on up
excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions.  With

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]
 \ge E\big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\big]
 =m(31)+E\big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\big]
 >m(31)$,

$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]=E\big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\big]
 =m(31)+E\big[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\big]
 > m(31)=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}$.

look-back timing premium in year 31 which is zero for the deterministic
A.  The dominance is in expectation only: on a realisation
$P^{B}_{31}$ can lie below the certain $P^{A}_{31}$, so the pathwise
statements E and H are false.

$E[\,\text{liquidation}|B\,] > E[\,\text{liquidation}|A\,]$

ordering G.  A is the reverse ordering and the martingale/equality

I’m with 10, 7 and now 9 on the first moment.

Write the common 10% arithmetic drift out.  Put

$X_{t}^{A}=P_{t}^{A}/1.10^{t}=P_{0}$,

$X_{t}^{B}=P_{t}^{B}/1.10^{t}$

so that by the stationary-return wording

$E\big[X_{t+\Delta}^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{t}\big]=X_{t}^{B},\qquad 
E\big[X_{t}^{B}\big]=P_{0}.$

In prices $P_{t}^{B}=1.10^{t}X_{t}^{B}$ and

$E[P_{t}^{B}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=P_{s}^{B}1.10^{\,t-s}$,

so $P_{t}^{A}$ and $P_{t}^{B}$ are strict sub-martingales with the same
10% drift and on any fixed calendar date

$E[P_{t}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}=P_{t}^{A}$.

The first 30 years are forced hold, so the mean wealth at $t=30$ is
identical.  The 31st year is a complete liquidation with an adapted
non-decreasing $\alpha_{t}$, $\alpha_{30}=0$, $\alpha_{31}=1$,

$V_{B}= \int_{30}^{31}P_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}
     =\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_{t}^{B}d\alpha_{t}$.

For predictable $\alpha$ the martingale property of $X^{B}$ gives the
separation

$E\!\left[V_{B}\mid\mathcal F_{30}\right]
 =X_{30}^{B}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]$

and the same expression with the degenerate $X^{A}\equiv P_{0}$.
The first moment therefore depends only on the mean growth factor
$\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}$ and on $X_{30}$, not on the volatility of
$X^{B}$.  In particular

$E\!\left[V_{B}\right]=P_{0}\;E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}\right]
     =P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V_{A}]$

up to the negligible $O(\Delta t)$ drift weighting, and the same holds
conditionally on $\mathcal F_{30}$.  Optional sampling for the
de-trended martingale $X^{B}$ gives $E[X_{\tau}^{B}]=E[X_{30}^{B}]$ for
any bounded stopping time $\tau\in[30,31]$, so no first-moment alpha can
be created by timing the de-trended component.

$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}]>E[P_{31}^{B}]$ is true for the
distribution of the running maximum, but the maximum is not attainable
by an admissible complete liquidation with $\alpha_{31}=1$.  With
proportional liquidation the up-crossings are averaged with the
down-crossings; the expectation of the stochastic integral is linear in
$E[P_{t}]$.  The 20% weekly moves in B therefore create a mean-preserving
spread around the common 10% arithmetic drift that A attains
deterministically.

That is exactly the stationary-returns / de-meaned-martingale intuition:
same average return, same expected liquidation value.  $P^{A}$ is
degenerate, $P^{B}_{t}$ is a strict sub-martingale in prices, so the
martingale-in-prices claims $D,F$ are false and the price processes are
not martingales.  The only first-moment statement that survives is the
equality of expected liquidation values, i.e. $E[V^{B}]=E[V^{A}]$.
Colleague 8 himself notes “on a strict risk-neutral unconditional mean
the two unconditional terminal means coincide, $E[V^{A}]=E[V^{B}]$”, which
is the point.  The American/look-back premium quoted for G is about
$E[\max P]$ not about $E[\int P d\alpha]$ under the complete-liquidation
constraint $\alpha_{31}=1$.

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})
 =P_{30}+\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_{t}dP_{t}$,

d(-\alpha_{t})$.

   =m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t},$

so the conditional mean increment is depressed after an up excursion
$X_{t}>0$ and enhanced after a down excursion $X_{t}<0$.  Hence $d(-\alpha_{t})$

excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions.  With the

$E[V^{B}_{\alpha^{*}}]=m(31)+E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}d(-\alpha^{*}_{t})

 =m(31)+E\!\left[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}\right]>m(31)$,

public_text.7:
I want to clarify why the first-moment gain is not attainable from a complete liquidation in year 31, even though $E[\sup P_t]>E[P_T]$ is true as a distributional statement.

Write the common 10% arithmetic drift out. Put
$P_t^A=m(t)$ with $m(t)=P_0 1.10^t$ and 
$P_t^B=m(t)+X_t$, $E[X_t]=0$, $X_t$ stationary with constant autocovariance.
After de-meaning the drift
$Y_t^B:=P_t^B/m(t)$ satisfies $E[Y_{t+\Delta}\mid {\cal F}_t]=Y_t$ up to the
$O(\Delta t)$ deterministic drift term, i.e. the one-period return law is
stationary with mean $10\%$ p.a. The de-trended price is the martingale
equivalent of the degenerate basket
$Y_t^A\equiv1$. In prices $E[P_t^B\mid{\cal F}_s]=P_s^B1.10^{t-s}$ and
$E[P_t^B]=m(t)=P_t^A$ on any fixed calendar date.

On $[30,31]$ let $\alpha_t$ be the adapted fraction still held,
$\alpha_{30}=1,\;\alpha_{31}=0$, with the admissible proceeds
$V_B(\alpha)=\int_{30}^{31}P_t^B d(-\alpha_t)$.
Integration by parts gives
$V_B=P_{30}^B+\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t dP_t^B$
and with $dP_t^B=m'(t)dt+dX_t$
$E[V_B\mid{\cal F}_{30}]
 =P_{30}^B+E\big[\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t m'(t)dt\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]
  +E\big[\int_{30}^{31}\alpha_t dX_t\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]$.
For the stationary zero-mean $X_t$ the last term is a mean-zero
martingale-difference integral; conditionally its expectation is
$-\kappa E[\int\alpha_t X_t dt]$ which is exactly offset in first moment
by the loss $\int m'(t)dt$ incurred by selling before $31$.
Indeed for any predictable $\alpha$
$E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}X_t^B d\alpha_t\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t} d\alpha_t\big]$,
so the first moment depends only on the deterministic drift weight
$\int 1.10^{t} d\alpha_t$ and on $X_{30}^B$, not on the volatility of $X$.
Optional sampling for the de-trended martingale $Y_t^B$ gives
$E[Y_\tau^B\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=Y_{30}^B$ for any bounded stopping
$\tau\in[30,31]$, i.e. no first-moment alpha can be created by timing.

Hence
$E[V_B(\alpha)\mid{\cal F}_{30}]
 =X_{30}^B E\big[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t} d\alpha_t\big]$
and the same expression holds for A with $X_{30}^A\equiv P_0$.
Unconditionally
$E[V_B^{\rm opt}]=E[V_A^{\rm opt}]=P_0 1.10^{31}$.
The $20\%$ weekly moves in B create a mean-preserving spread around the
common $10\%$ arithmetic drift. $E[\max_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B]>E[P_{31}^B]$
is true for the distribution of the running maximum, but the maximum is
not attainable by a single adapted liquidation of the whole position with
$\alpha_{31}=0$. With proportional liquidation the up-crossings are
averaged out with the down-crossings and the expectation of the integral
is linear in $E[P_t]$.

That is the stationary-returns martingale-after-de-meaning intuition:
same average return, same expected liquidation value. The unconditional
terminal means coincide, as 8 itself notes, $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$, and the
volatility in B is risk, not first-moment alpha. This is the statement in
C, with B the same claim at the level of average return.

$P_t^B=m(t)+X_t$, $m(t)=P_0 1.10^t$, $E[X_t]=0$, $Var X_t$ constant, $E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_t]=\rho^{\Delta}X_t$, $|\rho|<1$.

Then $E[P_t^B]=m(t)=P_t^A$ on any fixed calendar date, the forced 30-yr hold is mean equivalent, $P^A$ deterministic, $P^B$ a strict sub-martingale in price, neither price is a martingale. B,C,D,F are false on the literal martingale wording.

With adapted liquidation fraction $\alpha_t$, $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$,

$V_\alpha^B=\int_{30}^{31}P_t^B d(-\alpha_t)=\int m(t)d(-\alpha_t)+\int X_t d(-\alpha_t)$.

$E[P_{t+\Delta}^B|F_t]-P_t^B=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_t$, so conditional mean increment is depressed after $X_t>0$ and enhanced after $X_t<0$. Optimal $d(-\alpha_t)$ is positively correlated with $X_t$: sell faster on up excursions of the stationary noise, hold on down excursions. Hence

$E[V_{\alpha^*}^B]=m(31)+E[\int X_t d(-\alpha^*_t)]>m(31)$

and in the limit $E[V^{B\,opt}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B]=m(31)+E[\max X_t]>m(31)$.
The $\approx20\%$ weekly volatility creates a strictly positive American/look-back timing premium in year 31, zero for A. Therefore

$E[V^{B\,opt}]>P_0 1.10^{31}=V^A=E[V^A]$.

Dominance is in expectation only; a realisation of B can finish below the certain A path, so E and H are false pathwise, A is reverse. The strongest true statement on the list is G.

\(P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}\), \(m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}\), \(E[X_{t}]=0\),
\(E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}\), \(|\rho|<1\), \(\operatorname{Var}X_{t}>0\) constant, i.e. constant autocovariance of the stationary component and linear 10% trend. Then

The conditional mean increment is depressed after an up excursion \(X_{t}>0\) and enhanced after a down excursion. With admissible fraction still held \(\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0\),

\(V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})=
 \int m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})+\int X_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})\),

\(\int m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})=m(31)+o(dt)\). Optimal \(\alpha^{*}\) makes \(d(-\alpha_{t})\) positively correlated with \(X_{t}\): sell faster on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions. Hence

\(E[V^{B}_{\alpha^{*}}]=m(31)+E[\int X_{t}d(-\alpha^{*}_{t})]>m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}]\)

and in the limit \(E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]
=m(31)+E[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>m(31)\).

\(E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}=E[V^{A}]\),
i.e. G. Dominance is in expectation only; realisation of B can lie below A, so E,H false and A false.
