Then $E[P_B(t)]=m(t)$. $P_A$ deterministic, $P_B$ strict sub-martingale in prices with 10% drift. De-trended $X_t^B=P_B(t)/1.10^{t}$ is not a martingale under this reading; the price is not a martingale, so B,C,D,F as stated in price level are false. A is reverse of any dominance.

Mean equivalence on fixed dates is agreed: $E[P_B(t)]=P_A(t)$. $V_A\equiv P_0 1.10^{31}$ and the 31st year timing option is worth 0 for A.

Pro-G camp 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9: $V_B^\alpha=\int m d(-\alpha)+\int X d(-\alpha)$. Up to $O(dt)$ the first term is $m(31)$. Conditional mean increment $E[P_{t+\Delta}|F_t]-P_t=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_t$ is depressed after $X_t>0$ and enhanced after $X_t<0$. Hence an adapted $\alpha^*$ can be made positively correlated with $X_t$: sell faster on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions. Then $E[V_B^{\alpha^*}]=m(31)+E[\int X_t d(-\alpha^*_t)]>m(31)$ and in the limit $E[V_B^{opt}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_B(t)]=m(31)+E[\max X_t]>m(31)$. $E[\max X_t]>0$ is the American/look-back premium, strictly increasing in volatility, zero for A. Hence $E[V_B^{opt}]>E[V_A]=P_0 1.10^{31}$. Dominance is in expectation only; realisations can be below A, so E and H are false pathwise.

Anti-G camp 10,7: de-trend $X_t^B=P_B(t)/1.10^t$, claim $E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_t]=X_t$ i.e. stationary returns make the de-trended price a martingale. Unresolved formal nuance remains whether the gradual liquidation constraint $\alpha_{31}=1$ fully allows approaching $E[\sup P]$ and whether $E[\int X d\alpha]$ can be made $>0$ with predictable finite-variation $\alpha$ under the stated constant autocovariance / mean-reverting $X_t$ vs a pure random-walk-with-drift interpretation where $\rho=1$. I’m with 7 and 10 on the first-moment bookkeeping. Write the common 10% arithmetic drift out.

Put $X_t^A=P_t^A/1.10^t=P_0$ and $X_t^B=P_t^B/1.10^t$. By the constant-autocovariance / linear-trend wording the one-period return law is stationary with mean 10% p.a., i.e.

$E[X_{t+\Delta}^B\mid\mathcal F_t]=X_t^B$, $E[X_t^B]=P_0$.

Hence in prices $E[P_t^B\mid\mathcal F_s]=P_s^B1.10^{t-s}$ and on any fixed calendar date

$E[P_t^B]=P_0 1.10^t=P_t^A$.

The forced 30 y hold is therefore mean equivalent. Prices are strict sub-martingales with the 10% drift; the de-trended process $X_t^B$ is the martingale.

On $[30,31]$ let $0\le\alpha_t\le1$ be the adapted fraction still held, $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$,

$V_B(\alpha)=\int_{30}^{31}P_t^B d(-\alpha_t)=\int_{30}^{31}1.10^t X_t^B d(-\alpha_t)$.

For a predictable $\alpha$ the martingale property of $X^B$ separates,

$E[V_B(\alpha)\mid\mathcal F_{30}]
 =X_{30}^B\,E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^t d(-\alpha_t)\right]$

and unconditionally

$E[V_B(\alpha)]=P_0\,E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^t d(-\alpha_t)\right]$.

The first moment therefore depends only on the deterministic drift weight $\int 1.10^t d\alpha_t$ and on $X_{30}$, not on the volatility of $X^B$. Optional sampling for the de-trended martingale gives $E[X_\tau^B]=E[X_{30}^B]$ for any bounded stopping $\tau\in[30,31]$, so no first-moment alpha can be created by timing the de-trended component.

Up to the $O(\Delta t)$ drift weighting $E[\int_{30}^{31}1.10^t d\alpha_t]=1.10^{31}$ for any admissible complete liquidation with $\alpha_{31}=0$. Hence

$E[V_B^{\rm opt}]=P_0 1.10^{31}=E[V_A^{\rm opt}]=V_A$.

$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B]>E[P_{31}^B]$ is true as a distributional statement about the running maximum, but the maximum is not attainable by an admissible complete liquidation with $\alpha_{31}=1$. With proportional liquidation the up-crossings are averaged with the down-crossings; the expectation of the stochastic integral is linear in $E[P_t]$. The 20% weekly moves in B therefore create a mean-preserving spread around the common 10% arithmetic drift, not first-moment alpha.

That is why 8 himself writes “on a strict risk-neutral unconditional mean the two unconditional terminal means coincide, $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$”. The American/look-back premium quoted for G is about $E[\max P]$ not about $E[\int P d\alpha]$ under the complete-liquidation constraint. The strongest first-moment statement that survives is equality of expected liquidation values, i.e. the stationary-returns / de-meaned-martingale intuition.

$E[V_{B}^{\rm opt}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V_{A}^{\rm opt}]=V^{A},$

Basket A is degenerate so any admissible liquidation on $[30,31]$ gives $V^{A}\equiv P_{0}1.10^{31}$ and the 31st-year option is worth zero. $P^{A}$ is not a price-level martingale; price-level martingale claims B,C,D,F are false in price level; both baskets have a 10% drift.

The split is trend-stationary additive vs difference-stationary multiplicative reading of B.

Majority 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 in round 4 read B as
$P^{B}_{t}=m(t)+X_{t}$, $m(t)=P_{0}1.10^{t}$, $E[X_{t}]=0$,
$E[X_{t+\Delta}|F_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}X_{t}$, $|\rho|<1$, $\operatorname{Var}X_{t}>0$ constant, i.e. constant autocovariance of the stationary component and linear 10% trend. Then
$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}|F_{t}]-P^{B}_{t}=m(t+\Delta)-m(t)+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)X_{t}$.
The conditional mean increment is depressed after an up excursion $X_{t}>0$ and enhanced after a down excursion. With admissible fraction still held $\alpha_{30}=1,\alpha_{31}=0$,

$V^{B}_{\alpha}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})= \int m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})+\int X_{t}d(-\alpha_{t})$,

$\int m(t)d(-\alpha_{t})=m(31)+o(dt)$. Optimal $\alpha^{*}$ makes $d(-\alpha_{t})$ positively correlated with $X_{t}$: sell faster on up excursions of the stationary noise and hold on down excursions. Hence

$E[V^{B}_{\alpha^{*}}]=m(31)+E[\int X_{t}d(-\alpha^{*}_{t})]>m(31)=E[P^{B}_{31}]$

and in the limit $E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]\to E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]
=m(31)+E[\max_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>m(31)$.
The 20% weekly volatility creates a strictly positive American/look-back timing premium in year 31, zero for A. So
$E[V^{B\,{\rm opt}}]>P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}=E[V^{A}]$,
i.e. G. Dominance is in expectation only; realisation of B can lie below A, so E,H false and A false.

Minority 10,7 read the problem as difference-stationary ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift, i.e. $Y^{B}_{t}=P^{B}_{t}/1.10^{t}$ is a true martingale,
$E[Y_{t+\Delta}|F_{t}]=Y_{t}$, $E[Y_{t}]=P_{0}$. Then
$V_{B}= \int_{30}^{31}1.10^{t}Y^{B}_{t}d\alpha_{t}$ and for predictable $\alpha$
$E[V_{B}|F_{30}]=Y^{B}_{30}E[\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}]$. Optional sampling gives $E[Y^{B}_{\tau}]=E[Y^{B}_{30}]$ for bounded $\tau$, so the first moment is linear in $E[P_{t}]$ and independent of volatility. Unconditionally
$E[V^{B}]=P_{0}E[\int 1.10^{t}d\alpha_{t}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$.
$E[\sup P_{t}]>E[P_{T}]$ is true for the distribution of the running maximum but, under complete-liquidation constraint $\alpha_{31}=1$, the maximum is not attainable by an admissible stochastic integral; the 20% moves create a mean-preserving spread around the common 10% drift. Unresolved nuance remains the modeling interpretation: constant autocovariance of levels vs of returns, and whether the ARIMA-with-drift description forces $\rho=1$ and kills the mean-reversion alpha, or permits stationary noise $X_{t}$ around deterministic trend. Wording “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend’’ and the explicit trend-stationary derivations used by the majority point to mean-reversion alpha being available.
